[[Category:Chemical battery]]
A '''chemical battery''' is a [[battery]] that stores energy as [[chemical energy]].<ref>{{#cite:Q4245}}</ref>

== Simplest form ==

* [[Galvanic cell]]

== Classification and applications ==

* [[Primary battery]]
* [[Secondary battery]]

== Cell ==

A '''cell''' is the smallest [[functional unit]] of a chemical battery, consisted of two [[solid oxide fuel cell|electrodes]] submerged in [[electrolytes]].

A chemical battery consists '''one or more cells'''.

<ref>{{#cite:Q4245}}</ref>

== Charging and discharging ==

=== Discharge ===

==== Potential ====

===== Theoretical =====

The '''[[electric potential]]''' of a '''single cell''' of a chemical battery

$$
E_\text{cell}=E^\circ_\text{cathode}-E^\circ_\text{anode}
$$

where $E^\circ$ denotes the [[standard reduction potential]].
<ref>{{#cite:Q4245}}</ref>

===== Actual =====

The actual potential is often much lower than the theoretical potential in any given cell, due to

* [[polarisation]];
* internal resistance;
* non-standard state when significantly discharged.

To obtain the desired potential for practical applications, practical chemical batteries consist of many cells connected in series.

<ref>{{#cite:Q4245}}</ref>

=== Charging ===

Some chemical batteries, known as '''[[secondary batteries]]''', are rechargeable by the application of an external [[electric voltage]].

Due to [[polarisation]], the potential required to charge a [[secondary battery]] is often much higher than its discharging potential.

<ref>{{#cite:Q4245}}</ref>

== Capacity ==

The '''capacity''' of a single cell is given by

$$
Q=xnF
$$

<div class="center">
{| class="wikitable"
|-
| $Q$
| Battery capacity
|-
| $x$
| [[Valency]]
|-
| $n$
| Amount of active components in [[moles]]
|-
| $F$
| [[Faraday constant]]
|}
</div>

<ref>{{#cite:Q4245}}</ref>

=== Capacity-per-unit-mass ===

The '''capacity-per-unit-mass''' of a single cell is

$$
\frac{Q}{m},
$$

where $m$ is the [[mass]] of the battery.

<ref>{{#cite:Q4245}}</ref>

== Specific energy density ==

The '''total energy''' stored in a battery cell is

$$
E=\int I(t)V(t)dt
$$

The '''specific energy desntiy''' is therefore

$$
\frac{E}{m}
$$

<ref>{{#cite:Q4245}}</ref>

== Power density ==

Power density 

$$
\frac{P_\text{functional}}{m}
$$

is the functional power that can be derived per unit weight.

<ref>{{#cite:Q4245}}</ref>
